title: The Candle of Vision
author: AE (George William Russell)
tradition: Irish Theosophical mysticism (Dublin Hermetic / Theosophical Society circle)
locator_hints: Chapter 'Meditation' (c. 11-15% into file): the concentration exercise, 'five minutes of this effort', the upheaval it causes, initial 'stupor', 'the dark caverns of the brain begin to grow luminous'
Chapter 'The Many-Coloured Land', opening (c. 16%): 'a growing luminousness in my brain ... Normally we close our eyes on a cloudy gloom'
Chapters 'The Memory of Earth', 'Imagination', 'Dreams', 'The Architecture of Dream': his analysis of whether the pictures are memory, imagination or perception
'Retrospect' and 'The Earth Breath': lying on the hillside with shut eyes
summary: A poet-painter's first-person account of how his visions began and his attempt to analyse them. In 'Meditation' he gives the method: alone, choose a mental object, 'an abstraction of form', and hold the mind fixed on it without an instant's wavering, as a daily ritual; five minutes of it is harder than a ploughman's labour, and persistence stirs up violent passions. He then describes 'fiery brooding' on the infinite Self. At first there is only stupor, like stepping from day into a cavern; after weeks or months 'the dark caverns of the brain begin to grow luminous'. He attributes to this practice 'a growing luminousness in my brain as if I had unsealed in the body a fountain of interior light', contrasting the ordinary cloudy gloom behind closed eyes with the lit, coloured field in which figures and landscapes then appeared, typically lying with shut eyes on a hillside. Later chapters argue the pictures are seen, not composed.
why_relevant: Named practitioner's testimony tying a specific non-visual concentration practice to the onset, after weeks or months, of a luminous closed-eye field and perceived imagery.

date_evidence.basis: archive.org metadata date 1918 (London, Macmillan) for the Cornell copy; a 1920 reprint's copyright page reads 'First Edition October 1918'

found_via: seed lead; archive.org title search (the seed's Gutenberg pointer could not be confirmed through Gutenberg's search page)
notes: AE reports childhood and adolescent spontaneous visions too, so the causal claim for the practice is his own interpretation. The 'mental object' is held in the mind; whether it becomes seen is not stated in the passages skimmed.
